name: Stand up a Gateway
objective: CKA › Services & Networking. Drill EVERY corner of the Gateway API harder than the exam: install the CRDs, define a GatewayClass, stand up a Gateway with a named HTTP listener scoped by allowedRoutes, attach an HTTPRoute (path match + backend), add header-based matching, rewrite request headers with a filter, split traffic by weight across two backends, contrast with Ingress, and a no-hint diagnose-and-fix. Graded exactly, per requirement.

questions.title: Install the Gateway API CRDs
questions.teach:
The Gateway API isn't built into Kubernetes — it ships as **CRDs you install** from a release manifest. Until you `kubectl apply` them, the API server rejects `Gateway`/`HTTPRoute` objects.

**Gotcha:** wait for the CRD to reach the **Established** condition before creating CRs — applying a CRD and its CR together can race.
questions.prompt:
Install the Gateway API CRDs. The standard-channel manifest is staged at `/tmp/gateway-api-crds.yaml`. Apply it so the `GatewayClass`/`Gateway`/`HTTPRoute` types exist.

Target: the `gateways.gateway.networking.k8s.io` CRD is installed and reports the `Established` condition True.
questions.hint: `kubectl apply -f /tmp/gateway-api-crds.yaml`, then `kubectl get crd | grep gateway.networking.k8s.io`.
questions.solution:
kubectl apply -f /tmp/gateway-api-crds.yaml
kubectl get crd gateways.gateway.networking.k8s.io
questions.eli5:
Think of Kubernetes as a phone that comes with a set of built-in apps. The Gateway API is **not** one of the built-in apps — it's an app you have to **install from the app store** before the phone even knows what it is.

Those "apps" are called **CRDs** (Custom Resource Definitions). A CRD teaches the Kubernetes API server a brand-new noun. Until you install the Gateway API CRDs, the word `Gateway` (or `HTTPRoute`, or `GatewayClass`) is gibberish — if you try to create one, the API server shrugs: *"no matches for kind Gateway."*

Installing is one command: you `kubectl apply` a big YAML file that someone published (here it's staged at `/tmp/gateway-api-crds.yaml`). That file defines all the new types at once.

After you apply, there's a tiny beat where the API server registers the new type. It flips a flag called **`Established`** to `True` when it's truly ready. You want to wait for that flag before you start creating Gateways, or you can hit a race where your Gateway is rejected because the type isn't finished registering yet.

**Watch out:**

- **Gateway API is not built in.** No apply = `Gateway`/`HTTPRoute` are unknown kinds and get rejected.
- **Wait for `Established: True`** on the CRD before creating any Gateway/HTTPRoute — applying a CRD and its custom resource in the same breath can race.
- There are **two "channels"** of the manifest: **standard** (stable: GatewayClass, Gateway, HTTPRoute) and **experimental** (adds alpha stuff like TCPRoute). This lab uses the **standard** channel.
- CRDs are **cluster-scoped** — installing them affects the whole cluster, not one namespace.
questions.deepDive:
## Installing the Gateway API CRDs — full rundown

### Mental model
The Gateway API is the successor to Ingress, but unlike Ingress it is **not** part of core Kubernetes. It ships as a set of **CustomResourceDefinitions (CRDs)** published by the `kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api` project. You install the CRDs (the *types*), then install a **controller** (the implementation), then create the *resources*. On the exam the CRDs and controller are usually pre-staged or the manifest is handed to you — your job is to apply it and confirm it registered.

### The resources the CRDs add
| Kind | Scope | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `GatewayClass` | Cluster | Template naming the controller (like `IngressClass`) |
| `Gateway` | Namespaced | The actual listener(s) — ports/protocols/hostnames |
| `HTTPRoute` | Namespaced | L7 routing rules attached to a Gateway |
| `GRPCRoute` | Namespaced | gRPC routing (standard channel, newer) |
| `ReferenceGrant` | Namespaced | Allow cross-namespace refs (e.g. route → Service in another ns) |
| `TCPRoute`/`UDPRoute`/`TLSRoute` | Namespaced | L4 routing (**experimental** channel only) |

### API group & version
All Gateway API objects live under the API group **`gateway.networking.k8s.io`**. The stable version is **`v1`** for `GatewayClass`, `Gateway`, `HTTPRoute`. Some kinds are still `v1beta1`/`v1alpha2`.

```bash
kubectl api-resources --api-group=gateway.networking.k8s.io
```

### Install
```bash
# Apply the standard-channel release manifest (bundles all stable CRDs).
kubectl apply -f /tmp/gateway-api-crds.yaml

# Upstream equivalent (version-pinned):
kubectl apply -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api/releases/download/v1.2.0/standard-install.yaml
```

### Standard vs Experimental channel
| Channel | Contains |
|---|---|
| **standard** | GA/stable: `GatewayClass`, `Gateway`, `HTTPRoute`, `GRPCRoute`, `ReferenceGrant` |
| **experimental** | Everything in standard **plus** alpha: `TCPRoute`, `UDPRoute`, `TLSRoute`, and alpha fields on stable kinds |

Pick **standard** unless a task explicitly needs TCP/UDP/TLS routes.

### Confirm the CRD is registered
A CRD is only usable once the API server reports the **`Established`** condition `True` (and `NamesAccepted` `True`).

```bash
# List installed Gateway API CRDs
kubectl get crd | grep gateway.networking.k8s.io

# Check the Established condition on the Gateway CRD
kubectl get crd gateways.gateway.networking.k8s.io \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions[?(@.type=="Established")].status}'; echo

# Or wait for it explicitly (great before scripting CR creation)
kubectl wait --for=condition=Established \
  crd/gateways.gateway.networking.k8s.io --timeout=60s
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Types don't exist until applied.** Creating a `Gateway` before the CRD is installed → `error: resource mapping not found ... no matches for kind "Gateway"`.
- **CRD/CR race.** Applying a CRD and its custom resource in one `kubectl apply` (or back-to-back) can fail with *"no matches for kind"* because the type isn't `Established` yet. `kubectl wait --for=condition=Established` first.
- **CRDs are cluster-scoped** — no `-n` namespace; they affect the entire cluster.
- **CRDs alone route nothing.** You still need a controller (the GatewayClass's `controllerName` implementation) for traffic to actually flow. In a bare install, Gateways may stay `Programmed: False` with no controller.
- Full CRD name is plural + group: `gateways.gateway.networking.k8s.io`, `httproutes.gateway.networking.k8s.io`, `gatewayclasses.gateway.networking.k8s.io`.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl apply -f /tmp/gateway-api-crds.yaml
kubectl get crd | grep gateway.networking.k8s.io
kubectl wait --for=condition=Established crd/gateways.gateway.networking.k8s.io
kubectl api-resources --api-group=gateway.networking.k8s.io
```

questions.title: GatewayClass — the infrastructure template
questions.teach:
A **GatewayClass** is cluster-scoped and names the **controller** that implements any `Gateway` referencing it, via `spec.controllerName` (a domain-prefixed path). It's the Gateway API's analogue to `IngressClass`.

**Gotcha:** `kubectl create` has **no generator** for Gateway API objects — write the YAML and `apply -f` it.
questions.prompt:
Create a cluster-scoped `GatewayClass` named `kindlab-gc` with `spec.controllerName` exactly `kindlab.io/gateway-controller`.

Target: GatewayClass `kindlab-gc` exists with controllerName `kindlab.io/gateway-controller`.
questions.hint: Apply a manifest: `apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1`, `kind: GatewayClass`, `metadata.name: kindlab-gc`, `spec.controllerName: kindlab.io/gateway-controller`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: GatewayClass
metadata:
  name: kindlab-gc
spec:
  controllerName: kindlab.io/gateway-controller
EOF

verification.description: GatewayClass kindlab-gc exists with controllerName kindlab.io/gateway-controller

questions.eli5:
Imagine you're ordering an elevator for a building. You don't build the elevator yourself — you pick a **brand** ("install me a *KoneCo* elevator"). The brand tells the building crew *which company* is going to actually show up and build and run the thing.

A **GatewayClass** is exactly that brand label. It's a cluster-wide object that says: *"any Gateway that references me should be built by this particular controller."* It points at the controller with a field called **`controllerName`** — a domain-style string like `kindlab.io/gateway-controller`. That string isn't a URL you visit; it's just a unique name that a running controller is watching for. When a controller sees a GatewayClass naming it, it says "that's me!" and takes ownership of every Gateway that uses that class.

If you've used **Ingress** before, GatewayClass is the twin of **IngressClass** — same idea: pick which implementation handles your traffic.

Creating one is just a small YAML file you `kubectl apply`. There's no shortcut `kubectl create gatewayclass` command — Gateway API objects don't have those handy generators, so you write the YAML.

**Watch out:**

- **No `kubectl create` generator exists** for Gateway API kinds. Write the YAML and `apply -f` it (or `kubectl create -f`).
- **`controllerName` must be exact.** It's a domain-prefixed path (e.g. `kindlab.io/gateway-controller`) and is **immutable** — you can't edit it later, you'd recreate the GatewayClass.
- **GatewayClass is cluster-scoped** — no namespace, no `-n` flag.
- A GatewayClass by itself does nothing visible; it's just a template a real controller claims. If no controller is watching that `controllerName`, Gateways using it won't get programmed.
questions.deepDive:
## GatewayClass — the infrastructure template

### Mental model
A **GatewayClass** is the cluster-scoped "type of Gateway" object. It names the **controller** that will implement any `Gateway` referencing it. It is the Gateway API's direct analogue to **`IngressClass`**. Think: *GatewayClass : Gateway :: IngressClass : Ingress :: StorageClass : PVC.* One class, many Gateways.

### The one field that matters: controllerName
```yaml
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: GatewayClass
metadata:
  name: kindlab-gc
spec:
  controllerName: kindlab.io/gateway-controller   # domain-prefixed path, immutable
```

- **`spec.controllerName`** is a domain-prefixed string (`<domain>/<path>`), e.g. `example.com/gateway-controller`. It is **not** a URL — it's an opaque identifier a running controller watches for.
- A controller process is configured to own one `controllerName`. When it sees a GatewayClass with that value, it "accepts" the class and then manages every `Gateway` whose `gatewayClassName` points at it.
- `controllerName` is **immutable** after creation.

### Optional fields
| Field | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `spec.controllerName` | **Required.** Which controller implements this class |
| `spec.parametersRef` | Optional ref to an implementation-specific config object (e.g. a CRD holding tuning params) |
| `spec.description` | Human-readable note |

### Status to check
The controller sets an `Accepted` condition once it adopts the class:
```bash
kubectl get gatewayclass kindlab-gc \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions[?(@.type=="Accepted")].status}'; echo
```

### How it fits the chain
```
GatewayClass (names controller)
    ▲ gatewayClassName
Gateway (listeners: port/protocol/host)
    ▲ parentRefs
HTTPRoute (rules → Services)
```

### Create it (no generator!)
```bash
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: GatewayClass
metadata:
  name: kindlab-gc
spec:
  controllerName: kindlab.io/gateway-controller
EOF

kubectl get gatewayclass
kubectl get gatewayclass kindlab-gc -o yaml
```

### GatewayClass vs IngressClass
| | IngressClass | GatewayClass |
|---|---|---|
| Scope | Cluster | Cluster |
| Names controller via | `spec.controller` | `spec.controllerName` |
| Referenced by | `ingressClassName` on Ingress | `gatewayClassName` on Gateway |
| Default marker | `ingressclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class` annotation | *no default concept* — Gateways must name a class |

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **No `kubectl create gatewayclass` generator.** Gateway API kinds have no imperative generators; author YAML and `kubectl apply -f`. (Contrast: Ingress *does* have `kubectl create ingress`.)
- **`controllerName` is exact and immutable.** A typo means you delete and recreate; you cannot `kubectl edit` it.
- **Cluster-scoped** — never pass `-n`/`--namespace`.
- A GatewayClass with no matching controller stays effectively unused — Gateways referencing it won't reach `Programmed: True`. The object still *exists*, which is all the exam usually grades.
- Unlike IngressClass there is **no "default" GatewayClass**: every Gateway must explicitly set `gatewayClassName`.

### Quick reference
```yaml
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: GatewayClass
metadata: { name: kindlab-gc }
spec:
  controllerName: kindlab.io/gateway-controller
```
```bash
kubectl get gatewayclass kindlab-gc -o yaml   # verify controllerName + Accepted
```

questions.title: Gateway with a named listener + allowedRoutes
questions.teach:
A **Gateway** is namespaced. It references a class via `spec.gatewayClassName` and declares **listeners** — each with a unique `name`, a `protocol`, and a `port`. A listener's `allowedRoutes.namespaces.from: Same` restricts which namespaces may attach routes.

**Gotcha:** listener `name`s must be unique within a Gateway, and the `name` is what an HTTPRoute targets via `parentRefs[].sectionName`.
questions.prompt:
In namespace `gw-learn`, create a `Gateway` named `web-gw` referencing class `kindlab-gc` with ONE listener: `name: http`, `protocol: HTTP`, `port: 80`, and `allowedRoutes.namespaces.from: Same`.

Target: Gateway `web-gw` in `gw-learn`, gatewayClassName `kindlab-gc`, listener named `http` protocol HTTP port 80 with allowedRoutes.namespaces.from=Same.
questions.hint: `spec.gatewayClassName: kindlab-gc`; `spec.listeners: [{name: http, protocol: HTTP, port: 80, allowedRoutes: {namespaces: {from: Same}}}]`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: web-gw
  namespace: gw-learn
spec:
  gatewayClassName: kindlab-gc
  listeners:
  - name: http
    protocol: HTTP
    port: 80
    allowedRoutes:
      namespaces:
        from: Same
EOF

verification.description: Gateway web-gw: class kindlab-gc + listener http HTTP:80 allowedRoutes from=Same

questions.eli5:
Picture a building's **front desk**. A **Gateway** is that front desk: it's where outside traffic actually enters. The desk has one or more **windows** open — each window is a **listener** that says *"I accept this kind of visitor on this door number."* A window declares a `name`, a `protocol` (like HTTP), and a `port` (like 80).

The Gateway itself lives *inside a namespace* (unlike the GatewayClass, which was cluster-wide). It points back at its "brand" with `gatewayClassName: kindlab-gc` so the right controller builds it.

Each window also has a **guest policy** called `allowedRoutes`. Setting `allowedRoutes.namespaces.from: Same` means *"only accept route-cards from people in **this same namespace**."* It's a security fence: it controls **who is allowed to plug their routing rules into this window.** The options are `Same` (this namespace only), `All` (anyone), or `Selector` (only namespaces matching a label).

Finally, each window has a **unique name** (`http`). That name matters a lot later: when you write an HTTPRoute, it targets a specific window by that name using `sectionName`.

**Watch out:**

- **Listener `name`s must be unique** within a Gateway. Duplicates are rejected.
- The listener **`name` is the handle** an HTTPRoute uses via `parentRefs[].sectionName` — get it wrong and the route won't attach.
- **`allowedRoutes.namespaces.from`** defaults to `Same` if you omit it. Using `All` lets routes from *any* namespace attach; `Selector` needs a label selector block.
- **Gateway is namespaced** (needs `-n`), but **GatewayClass is cluster-scoped** — don't mix them up.
- A Gateway with no running controller won't get an address or reach `Programmed: True`; the object still exists, which is usually what's graded.
questions.deepDive:
## Gateway with a named listener + allowedRoutes

### Mental model
A **Gateway** is the namespaced object that represents the actual traffic entry point (the "front door" + its ports). It references a `GatewayClass` to pick its implementation, then declares one or more **listeners** — each a `(name, protocol, port, [hostname], [tls], [allowedRoutes])` tuple. Routes (`HTTPRoute`) attach *to a specific listener* and the controller programs the dataplane.

```
GatewayClass ──gatewayClassName──▶ Gateway ──listener "http"──▶ attached HTTPRoutes
```

### Minimal manifest
```yaml
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: web-gw
  namespace: gw-learn
spec:
  gatewayClassName: kindlab-gc
  listeners:
  - name: http            # unique within this Gateway; HTTPRoute targets it via sectionName
    protocol: HTTP
    port: 80
    allowedRoutes:
      namespaces:
        from: Same        # Same | All | Selector
```

### Listener fields
| Field | Required | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | ✅ | **Unique** per Gateway; HTTPRoute's `parentRefs[].sectionName` references it |
| `protocol` | ✅ | `HTTP`, `HTTPS`, `TLS`, `TCP`, `UDP` |
| `port` | ✅ | Listener port (e.g. 80, 443) |
| `hostname` | ❌ | Restrict listener to a host (supports `*.example.com` wildcard) |
| `tls` | for HTTPS/TLS | `mode: Terminate\|Passthrough` + `certificateRefs` (Secret) |
| `allowedRoutes` | ❌ | Which routes may attach (see below) |

### allowedRoutes.namespaces.from
| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **`Same`** | Only routes **in the Gateway's own namespace** may attach *(default)* |
| **`All`** | Routes from **any** namespace may attach |
| **`Selector`** | Only namespaces matching `allowedRoutes.namespaces.selector` (a label selector) |

You can also restrict **which kinds** attach via `allowedRoutes.kinds` (e.g. only `HTTPRoute`).

```yaml
    allowedRoutes:
      namespaces:
        from: Selector
        selector:
          matchLabels: { team: web }
      kinds:
      - kind: HTTPRoute
```

### How a route targets a listener
An HTTPRoute's `parentRefs` points at the Gateway by `name` (+ `namespace` if cross-ns) and optionally a **`sectionName`** equal to the **listener name**:
```yaml
# on the HTTPRoute
parentRefs:
- name: web-gw
  sectionName: http      # must equal the listener's name
```
Omitting `sectionName` attaches to **all compatible listeners**; setting it pins to one.

### Status to verify
```bash
kubectl -n gw-learn get gateway web-gw
# Conditions worth reading:
#   Accepted   = config is valid / listener names OK
#   Programmed = controller provisioned the dataplane (needs a real controller)
kubectl -n gw-learn get gateway web-gw \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions[*].type}{"\n"}'
kubectl -n gw-learn get gateway web-gw \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.listeners[*].name}{"\n"}'
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Listener names must be unique** within the Gateway; duplicates → `Accepted: False`.
- The **listener `name` is the contract** with HTTPRoute (`sectionName`). Mismatch → route not attached (`NoMatchingParent`).
- **`from: Same` is the default.** To accept cross-namespace routes you must set `All` or `Selector` — and the *route* often also needs a `ReferenceGrant` for cross-namespace **backends**.
- **Gateway is namespaced** (`-n`), **GatewayClass is cluster-scoped** (no `-n`).
- **HTTPS/TLS listeners** need `tls.certificateRefs` → a Secret; forgetting it blocks programming.
- No controller behind the GatewayClass → Gateway may stay `Programmed: False` with no address, even though the object is valid.

### Quick reference
```yaml
spec:
  gatewayClassName: kindlab-gc
  listeners:
  - { name: http, protocol: HTTP, port: 80, allowedRoutes: { namespaces: { from: Same } } }
```
```bash
kubectl -n gw-learn get gateway web-gw -o yaml   # check listeners + status conditions
```
